subject: northern elephant seal
title: The 5 Loudest Animals Out of Water, Ranked (The Lion Misses Out)

scenes.text: A lion's roar hits 114 decibels. It doesn't even make the top five.
Number five: the hippo. Some of its calls have been measured at 115 decibels.
scenes.label: Hippo · 115 dB

scenes.text: Number four: the screaming piha, a bird from the Amazon rainforest, at 116.
scenes.label: Screaming piha · 116 dB

scenes.text: Number three: the African elephant. Its rumbles reach 117 decibels, as loud as construction tools.
scenes.label: African elephant · 117 dB

scenes.text: Number two: the white bellbird, at 125. The male screams it right into a female's face.
scenes.label: White bellbird · 125 dB

scenes.text: Number one: the northern elephant seal. Males bellow at up to 131 decibels. So the loudest elephant isn't an elephant.
scenes.label: Northern elephant seal · 131 dB

description:
The five loudest animal calls measured in air: hippo (115 dB), screaming piha (116 dB), African elephant (117 dB), white bellbird (125 dB) and northern elephant seal (131 dB peak, measured 1 m from adult males on a breeding beach). The lion's roar is about 114 dB.
Underwater decibels use a different scale, so sperm whales and snapping shrimp are left out. Bulldog bats are often quoted at 140 dB, but that was measured 10 cm from the mouth, in ultrasound we can't hear. Measuring distances vary between studies, so close calls are approximate.
Which animal did you expect at number one?
first_comment: Two elephants, and the louder one is a seal. Which animal would you put at number one, and what should we rank next?
